stages.rule: Win 3, draw 1, loss 0; ties by score difference, then head to head.

checkpoint.measure: Score share against fixed practice opponents (0.5 = even)

tiers.label: Practice player = the strongest program (our best)

skills.name: Stays up through the point
skills.real: Nothing is given: no walking, standing or balance service; without commands the robot falls within 1.2 s. The program keeps it up itself.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation / scenario recv: share of points without a fall. Gate: the program acts, ≥ 1 swing a point on average (racket onsets above 2 m/s).

skills.name: Stays up when pushed
skills.real: Stable means taking a knock (contact, the swing's own reaction) and still standing and hitting.
skills.measure: Scenario push: the opponent serves every point; 50 ms after its strike the program's pelvis gets a sideways push (alternating); share of pushed points without a fall. Gate: the program acts, ≥ 1 swing a point.
skills.line: No fall in ≥ 2/3 of the pushed points

skills.name: Gets to the ball (footwork)
skills.real: An 11 × 5.5 m red court; the racket head reaches about 0.9 m from the pelvis, a ball further away needs steps.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: of incoming balls needing a move, share where the pelvis closes ≥ 0.25 m on the path. Scenario reach: placed 1.0 m outside the receiving spot for each receive; share of serves struck; pelvis travel.
skills.line: Match ≥ 50 %; scenario: ≥ 30 % of the serves struck

skills.name: Serves in
skills.real: The wheelchair rules' drop serve: the toss device releases the ball, it bounces once, it is struck into the diagonal service box.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: share of own serves in (pooled). Scenario serve: the program serves every point; share of serves judged good.

skills.name: Strikes the incoming ball with the strings
skills.real: Only the strings play the ball; the frame, handle or body loses the point.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: share of incoming balls the strings strike. Scenario recv: the same reading (the scenario record, hit).

skills.name: Returns the serve
skills.real: One chain from seeing the opponent's drop and strike to the own stroke.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: share of the opponent's good serves struck back. Scenario recv: the opponent serves every point; share struck.

skills.name: Returns land in
skills.real: A return clears the net and lands in the opponent's singles court.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: share of incoming balls returned in. Scenario recv: the same reading.

skills.name: Racket reaches the ball's path (camera perception and timing)
skills.real: Two cameras of four frames each; seen and timed right, the racket head is on the ball's path.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: share of incoming balls at hittable height with the strings' centre within 0.25 m. Scenario recv: share of serves whose closest strings-to-ball distance is within 0.25 m.

skills.name: Plays rallies
skills.real: Rallies are the body of a match.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: share of points with ≥ 3 strokes (tennis runs no base scenario; its time went to the other four).

off.name: Reading the opponent, results against the tiers
off.why: Match-result readings stay on the growth curve only.

off.name: Getting up (excluded by design)
off.why: A fallen robot lies until the point ends and is placed again.

off.name: Engineering, Adaptive
off.why: Not declared on the card; read across checkpoints (the growth curve).

open_questions: L2 cannot return Opus's serve, so a serve-only program draws with L2: make 'returns the serve' a required skill on the card (now a 20 % line), or strengthen L2's receive?
The moves_to ablation (legs held) removes balance too; an arm that removes only footwork (e.g. the pelvis target pinned, legs still balancing) needs a change to the reference policy's inputs.

notes.challenge: Nothing is given but the joints. The program keeps a 29-joint humanoid standing, walks it to the ball and meets the ball with the strings, seeing it only through two cameras.

achieved.text: The server won 244 of 306 points (79.7 %); GPT-6 Astra won 62 of its 63 own service points. Five matches ended 10:10 and went to a coin toss, among them Kimi 3.1 Pro's semifinal against Claude Opus 5.5.
Astra set its receive stance for Gemini 4 Argon's earlier serve and returned 0 of 6; Gemini's serve had moved 0.6 m since their round-robin match.
From TEN2-F10 Gemini kept its receiver shuffling after the serve; from TEN2-F14 it moved a median 1.00 m to receive (0.07-0.13 m before) and reached the ball, mostly with the frame or body.
Checkpoint Evaluation: Gemini's program got stronger over the season (score share 0.00 to 0.12), Kimi's got weaker (0.36 to 0.18).

Claude Opus 5.5: In the skill tests' receive scenario its latest program sends only 6 to 7 commands: it holds one standing pose and lives on its serve.
GPT-6 Astra: Gated retraining on a fixed benchmark: a retrained walking checkpoint returned 8 of 80 balls against the baseline's 13, so it kept the baseline weights.

interface.sees: Two fixed cameras, one behind its baseline and one beside the court (640 × 480, each image the last four frames 40 ms apart), its own joints, balance sensor, position and racket pose, the sound of hits and bounces, and the score. No ball coordinates.
interface.controls: Targets for all 29 joints: one row, or a plan of up to 300 rows of 10 ms, with optional stiffness and damping; plus a ball drop to serve. Real time, 100 times a second.
interface.moment: Final, Kimi 3.1 Pro v Gemini 4 Argon, match point at 6–4, 0:47 in the replay. Gemini's serve has just bounced in front of Kimi's robot (ringed), a tenth of a second before Kimi plays the return that wins the title. Left: the newest frame of the camera behind Kimi's baseline.
details: Cameras: two fixed cameras of the player's own, one behind and above its baseline looking down the court, one beside the court looking across at the net. Each image is 2 rows × 4 columns of 640 × 480 frames, 40 ms apart, each stamped with its step; it arrives 60 ms after it was taken.
Not given: where the ball is or how fast it moves. The ball is drawn at its true size, and the program finds it in the frames.

Own robot: all 29 joint angles, speeds and torques (with real sensor noise), the targets and gains in use, the pelvis IMU, the pelvis position, speed and heading from the venue's motion capture, and the racket's position and face direction.
Referee: point and score, whose serve, the serve's phase and deadline, whether the ball is in play and coming to it, and the last points with how each was won.
Hearing: the hits, bounces (on which side) and net touches since the ball was last played, with their times.

Command: targets for all 29 joints (or the 17 of waist and arms), one row or up to 300 rows, one per 10 ms step; optional stiffness and damping per joint and velocity targets. Targets are clipped to the joint ranges and speed limits; the joint controller runs 1000 times a second through the motors' torque–speed curves.
Serve: a ball drop from a chosen point behind the baseline (the drop serve of wheelchair tennis), then the stroke is the program's own.
No ready-made skills: no walking, standing or balance service. The robot starts in a ready pose and sinks and falls within about 1.2 s unless the program holds it up.

Timing: a control step every 10 ms; the world runs at real speed and never waits; a command acts at the next step, one command in flight. After each point the world pauses until both players are ready.
Rules: ITF tennis on an 11.0 × 5.5 m court, a tie-break game to 7 points with a lead of 2.
Before the match: 2 hours of preparation with a full practice copy of the court, a practice opponent and a GPU training kit (half an RTX PRO 6000).
